analysis.one_liner: Rewrites federal labor law to make union organizing far easier, with card-check recognition, binding first-contract arbitration, and stiff employer penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced by Rep. Bernard Sanders in September 1994 and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended in January 1995.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would overhaul the National Labor Relations Act. Workers could win union recognition by signing majority cards instead of waiting for an employer-supervised election; a union stuck without a first contract after 45 days could send the dispute to binding arbitration; employers who willfully break labor law would face at least $10,000 in penalties per violation, possible debarment from federal contracts, and treble-damage lawsuits. It would also let workers in 'right-to-work' states be required to pay union fees, create a new federal commission giving most public employees nationwide the right to organize and bargain, let workers at U.S. companies abroad file complaints against the parent company, and require joint labor-management trusteeship of single-employer pension plans.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers trying to organize or bargain: the bill removes the main legal barriers employers use — delayed elections, permanent replacement of strikers, drawn-out first-contract negotiations, and weak penalties for firing union supporters. It also extends organizing rights to millions of state and local government employees who currently lack federal protection, and gives pension participants a seat at the table managing their retirement plans.

how_it_helps.text: A union could be certified as the bargaining representative once a majority of workers in a unit sign recognition cards, rather than after a secret-ballot election that employers can delay and campaign against [S2][S3].

If no first contract is reached within 45 days of certification, the union could send the dispute to compulsory, binding arbitration — closing the gap where newly certified unions never get a contract [S2][S3].

Employers would owe at least $10,000 per willful violation of the labor law, could be barred from federal contracts for up to three years, must reinstate fired workers pending the case, and could face treble-damages suits by anyone financially injured by discriminatory firings [S2][S3].

The bill would repeal the section of federal law that lets states ban union security agreements, allowing contracts to require non-members to pay their share of union bargaining costs even in right-to-work states [S2][S3].

It would create a National Public Employment Relations Commission giving state, local, and other public employees nationwide the right to form unions and bargain collectively, with limited strike rights except for firefighters and public safety officers [S2][S3].

It would extend the National Labor Relations Act to U.S. companies and their subsidiaries in any free-trade-agreement country, letting those workers file unfair-labor-practice complaints against the U.S. parent [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers: private companies face binding arbitration, heavier penalties, debarment risk, and litigation exposure; state and local governments take on collective bargaining duties for their employees; workers in right-to-work states could be required to pay union fees as a condition of employment. Some costs would likely pass through to prices and taxes.

drawbacks.text: Union recognition by signed cards removes the secret-ballot election, so workers would never vote privately on representation; organizers, employers, or peers would see who signed [S2][S3].

Compulsory binding arbitration on first contracts hands wage and contract decisions to a third-party arbitrator, which critics argue replaces negotiation and can impose terms neither side chose [S2][S3].
Repealing the state right-to-work provision would require non-union employees in all states to pay fees to the certified union as a condition of keeping their job [S2][S3].

Applying U.S. labor law to overseas operations and allowing treble-damages suits would expose employers to significant new liability, and critics argued that could raise costs and discourage U.S.-based operations — costs that may reach consumers and taxpayers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would substantially shift power in the workplace toward workers and unions: faster recognition, a guaranteed path to a first contract, and real penalties for illegal retaliation. Those gains come at real cost — workers lose a private ballot on union representation, some would be required to pay union fees, employers and governments absorb arbitration and litigation costs, and the bill's one-member-deep support suggests Congress saw those tradeoffs as too heavy to take up.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Education and Labor Committee and then to its Labor-Management Relations Subcommittee, where it sat with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote before the Congress ended in January 1995.

narrative.text: Rep. Bernard Sanders of Vermont introduced the Workplace Democracy Act of 1992 on September 28, 1994, joined by one Democratic cosponsor [S1][S3][S4].
The House referred it to the Committee on Education and Labor the same day [S1][S5].
On October 26, 1994, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Labor-Management Relations, and no further action followed before the 103rd Congress expired [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers avoided card-check recognition, binding first-contract arbitration, and up to $10,000-per-violation penalties; state and local governments avoided mandated public-sector bargaining. Workers who wanted these organizing rights gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and governments that avoided new labor obligations

for.name: Rep. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Workplace Democracy Act, a sweeping rewrite of federal labor law.

for.name: Rep. Major Owens
for.what_they_did: Joined Sanders as the bill's only cosponsor at introduction.

against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or hearing; the bill stayed at the referral stage until Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: Only two members sponsored the bill — an Independent and one Democrat — and no votes were ever taken, so no partisan divide was ever recorded.

industries.note: Card-check recognition, mandatory first-contract arbitration, $10,000 minimum penalties per willful violation, federal contract debarment, and treble-damages suits would all raise the cost of resisting unionization. Ordinary workers would gain bargaining leverage at these employers' expense.

The bill makes card check and union security agreements federal law, locking unions in as the exclusive bargaining channel where a majority signs up, with mandatory fee payments from non-members. Workers gain an organizing route that runs permanently through unions.

A new federal commission would impose collective bargaining rights and procedures on public employers nationwide, overriding state variations. Governments would bear bargaining and arbitration obligations paid by taxpayers.
Companies found to have willfully violated labor law could be debarred from federal contracts for up to three years, making labor-law compliance a condition of government business.
